title: Waves, Sound and Light
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Waves, Sound and Light Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Use wave and particle models to describe energy transfer through different mediums and examine the usefulness of each model for explaining phenomena (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on waves: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed, frequency and wavelength, sound in solids, liquids and gases, echoes, and reflection, refraction and absorption of light. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Sound needs particles to pass on vibrations; light can travel through a vacuum.
body_html:
How to think about it

A wave transfers energy without moving the material along with it.

  • Transverse waves (light, ripples) vibrate at right angles; longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate along the direction of travel.
  • Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Sound is faster in solids than in gases and cannot travel through a vacuum.
  • Light can be reflected, refracted (bent), absorbed or transmitted, and travels through space.
Example

Frequency 50 Hz, wavelength 2 m. Speed?

v = f × λ

50 × 2

Answer: 100 m/s

Example

Echo heard 2 s after a clap. Wall distance? (340 m/s)

340 × 2 = 680 m there and back

680 ÷ 2

Answer: 340 m

Common mistakes

  • Thinking sound can travel through a vacuum.
  • Thinking the wave carries the water or air along with it.
  • Forgetting to halve the distance in echo questions.

faq.q: What is the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves?
faq.a: In a transverse wave the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel. In a longitudinal wave they are along the direction of travel, making compressions and rarefactions.

faq.q: Why do we use both a wave model and a particle model?
faq.a: The particle model explains why sound needs a medium and travels faster in solids. The wave model explains frequency, wavelength, reflection and refraction.

items.q: Is a wave on a rope shaken up and down a transverse or a longitudinal wave?
c: neither: it is not a wave
items.e: Transverse: vibrations at right angles to the direction of travel. Longitudinal: vibrations along it.

items.q: Why does sound travel fastest in solids?
c: Particles are packed closely, so vibrations pass on quickly.
items.e: Sound is about 340 m/s in air and over 5000 m/s in steel.

items.q: A wave on a guitar string travels at 250 m/s with a frequency of 50 Hz. What wavelength did Harper calculate? (wavelength = speed ÷ frequency)
A wave on a spring toy travels at 15 m/s with a wavelength of 3 m. What frequency did Ruby calculate? (frequency = speed ÷ wavelength)
A doctor uses ultrasound to see an unborn baby. Why is ultrasound used?
c: High-frequency sound reflects from tissues and is safe.
It is a kind of X-ray.
items.e: Ultrasound is above human hearing (over 20 000 Hz).

items.q: Mia stands 170 m from a wall and claps. She hears the echo 1 s later. What speed of sound does this give?
items.e: The sound travels 340 m (there and back) in 1 s.

items.q: Zara measures how bright a torch looks through 1, 2, 3 and 4 sheets of tracing paper. What is she investigating?
c: how much light is transmitted and absorbed
items.e: Each sheet absorbs or scatters some light.

items.q: A wave travels at 30 m/s with a frequency of 20 Hz. What is its wavelength?
items.e: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency = 30 ÷ 20.

items.q: Humpback whales migrating along the Australian coast sing to each other. Why does their song travel a long way?
c: Sound travels quickly and far in water.
items.e: Water particles are closer than air particles.

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed? (wave speed = frequency × wavelength)
Jack shines a ray box into a glass block at different angles and measures how much it bends. What is the independent variable?
items.e: He changes the incoming angle.

items.q: Ethan hears an echo 0.4 s after making a sound with a ship's sonar. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water (sonar). How far away is the reflecting surface?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 = 1500 × 0.4 ÷ 2.

items.q: A black shirt feels hotter in the sun than a white shirt. Why?
c: Black absorbs more light energy; white reflects more.
items.e: Absorbed light is transferred to heat.

items.q: Kai measures a wave on a spring toy with a frequency of 2 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. What is the wave speed? (speed = frequency × wavelength)

A wave travels at 8 m/s with a frequency of 2 Hz. What is its wavelength?
items.e: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency = 8 ÷ 2.

items.q: Kai hears an echo 2 s after making a sound. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the reflecting surface?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 = 340 × 2 ÷ 2.

items.e: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency = 50 ÷ 100.

items.q: Noah hears an echo 0.6 s after making a sound with a ship's sonar. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water (sonar). How far away is the reflecting surface?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 = 1500 × 0.6 ÷ 2.

items.q: Ethan hears an echo 0.5 s after making a sound with a ship's sonar. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water (sonar). How far away is the reflecting surface?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 = 1500 × 0.5 ÷ 2.

items.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 0.5 s?
items.e: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 0.5 = 170 m.

items.q: A student claps near a wall and hears the echo 2 s later. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away is the wall?
items.e: The sound goes there and back: 330 × 2 = 660 m, so the wall is 330 m away.

items.q: A ray of light goes from air into a glass block at an angle. What happens or why?
c: It bends away from the normal.
Light refracts as it leaves the water.
It goes straight on without bending.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 55°. What is the angle of reflection?
items.e: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

items.q: A green car is lit only by red light. What colour does it look?
items.e: Objects reflect their own colour and absorb the others. If their colour is not in the light, they look black.

items.q: A black book is lit only by white light. What colour does it look?
items.e: Objects reflect their own colour and absorb the others. If their colour is not in the light, they look black.

items.q: A ray of light makes an angle of 50° with the surface of a mirror. What is the angle of incidence (measured from the normal)?
items.e: The normal is at 90° to the mirror, so 90° − 50° = 40°.

items.q: A red T-shirt is lit only by blue light. What colour does it look?
items.e: Objects reflect their own colour and absorb the others. If their colour is not in the light, they look black.

items.q: A ray of light enters a glass block along the normal (at 90° to the surface). What happens or why?
c: It goes straight on without bending.
It bends away from the normal.
Different colours refract by different amounts.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: A white hat is lit only by blue light. What colour does it look?

items.q: William shines a torch at a metal pan. What happens to the light?
c: It transmits no light; light is reflected or absorbed.
It transmits some light but scatters it, so things look blurry.
It transmits almost all light, so you can see clearly through it.
The light is turned into sound.
items.e: A metal pan is opaque.

items.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 65°. What is the angle of reflection?
items.e: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

items.q: What happens to light when it hits a mirror?
c: It is reflected; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
items.e: Smooth surfaces give clear reflections.

items.q: Which travels faster: light or sound?
items.e: This is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

items.q: In the spectrum made by a prism, which colour comes just before orange?
items.e: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

items.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 15°. What is the angle of reflection?
items.e: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).

It transmits some light but scatters it, so things look blurry.
It transmits no light; light is reflected or absorbed.
The light is turned into sound.

items.q: A prism splits white light into colours. What happens or why?
c: It bends away from the normal.
Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water.
Different colours refract by different amounts.
It goes straight on without bending.
items.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes speed going into a different material.

items.q: Ethan shines a torch at air. What happens to the light?
c: It transmits no light; light is reflected or absorbed.

It transmits almost all light, so you can see clearly through it.

items.q: In the spectrum made by a prism, which colour comes just before yellow?
items.e: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

items.q: A red hat is lit only by green light. What colour does it look?
items.e: Objects reflect their own colour and absorb the others. If their colour is not in the light, they look black.

items.q: What does the lens in the eye do?
items.e: Like a camera lens.

items.q: Why does a pinhole camera make an upside-down image?
c: Light travels in straight lines, so rays cross over at the pinhole.
items.e: Straight lines.

items.q: How fast does light travel in a vacuum?
c: it does not travel in a vacuum
items.e: Nothing travels faster.

items.q: Aarav's model: “Your voice bounces off a canyon wall.” Is the wave mainly reflected, absorbed or transmitted?
items.e: Waves can be reflected (bounce), absorbed (taken in, often as heat) or transmitted (pass through).

items.q: Why does the bottom of a swimming pool look closer than it is?
c: Light from the bottom refracts as it leaves the water.
Light reflects off the bottom twice.
items.e: Refraction.

items.q: Does sound travel faster in air or in steel?
items.e: Particles are closer together in solids.

items.q: Which is faster: light or sound?
c: light (about 300 000 000 m/s compared with about 340 m/s)
items.e: Lightning before thunder.

items.q: Why does a red apple look red in white light?
c: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours.
items.e: Coloured objects reflect their colour.

items.q: Why is a periscope made with two mirrors at 45°?
c: Each mirror reflects the light through 90°, so it comes out parallel to where it went in.
items.e: Law of reflection.

items.q: Priya's model: “You hear music from a car through its closed windows.” Is the wave mainly reflected, absorbed or transmitted?
items.e: Waves can be reflected (bounce), absorbed (taken in, often as heat) or transmitted (pass through).

items.q: Why are soft materials used to soundproof rooms?
c: They absorb sound instead of reflecting it.
items.e: Absorption.

items.q: Noah's model: “A heavy curtain makes a room quieter.” Is the wave mainly reflected, absorbed or transmitted?
items.e: Waves can be reflected (bounce), absorbed (taken in, often as heat) or transmitted (pass through).

items.q: What is refraction?
c: the bending of light as it passes from one material into another
items.e: It changes speed.

items.q: Ella makes a slinky wave by pushing and pulling one end. What kind of wave is this?
items.e: The coils move back and forth along the slinky.

items.q: Ruby's model: “Light bounces off a calm lake.” Is the wave mainly reflected, absorbed or transmitted?
items.e: Waves can be reflected (bounce), absorbed (taken in, often as heat) or transmitted (pass through).

items.q: Noah tests which material blocks the most sound from a buzzer: foam, cardboard or bubble wrap. What should he keep the same?
c: the buzzer, its distance from the sound meter and the thickness of each material
items.e: Only the material should change.

items.q: What happens when a wave hits a surface?
c: It can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
items.e: Depends on the material.

items.q: Why are emergency vehicles often yellow with reflective strips?
c: They reflect lots of light so they are easy to see.
items.e: Reflection for safety.
